items.title: Persist Guardian review failures for reports across restarts
items.body:
Persist Guardian review failures for reports across restarts

## Why

Failed Guardian review evidence was process-local, so restarting Codex lost the context needed for later diagnostic reports.

## What changed

- Persist failed-review records in SQLite before reviewer cleanup, retaining at most 64 records globally, eight per thread, and 8 MiB of evidence. Delete persisted evidence when its reviewed thread is deleted.
- Recover and deduplicate persisted and in-memory records for the reported task tree when uploading `auto-review-failures.jsonl`.
- Bound persistence attempts to 250 ms and retain an in-memory fallback when storage is unavailable. Keep capture gated by user opt-in and non-ephemeral sessions, and export evidence only when logs are included.

## Testing

Add coverage for persistence across reopen and process restart, retention limits, cascading deletion, busy-storage fallback, and report uploads with and without logs, including SQLite log failures.

items.title: Require hostname authorization before proxy DNS lookups
items.body:
Require hostname authorization before proxy DNS lookups

## Why

Resolving unapproved hostnames discloses them to DNS even when the proxy ultimately rejects the request. Allowing local binding in a managed macOS sandbox also granted direct outbound access to port `53`.

## What changed

- Require an allowlist match or policy approval before resolving a hostname for address checks.
- Recheck baseline restrictions after local and remote policy approval so approval cannot bypass explicit denies or local/private address restrictions.
- Preserve DNS checks for inner HTTPS requests after an approved CONNECT, including hosts without a persisted allowlist entry.
- Remove the Seatbelt allowance for external DNS while retaining local binding and loopback proxy access.

## Testing

Add regression tests for zero DNS lookups on unapproved hosts, private-address rejection after approval, local and remote approval ordering, and DNS checks after approved CONNECT requests. Add a macOS Seatbelt child test that verifies external UDP and TCP port `53` access is denied while local binding and proxy connectivity remain available.

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

OpenAI.Codex 26.1002.6548.0

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro 20x

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64

### What issue are you seeing?

Codex Desktop on Windows progressively accumulates repeated local Node/MCP/CUA/node_repl helper process batches while the same desktop app-server remains running.

The process count and private committed memory increase over time during normal multi-session Codex work. Eventually this creates severe Windows memory pressure and paging, and Codex sessions become dramatically slower.

In my workload, tasks that normally finish in tens of minutes can take 2–4 hours when multiple Codex/Claude sessions are active.

## Observed Codex process accumulation

During one long-running Codex Desktop app-server session, I measured:

- 200 Codex-owned Node-family processes in total
- 110 MCP-related Node processes
- 52 CUA Node processes
- 38 node_repl processes
- approximately 11.62 GB of private memory across those Node-family processes

The process creation timestamps showed repeated batches throughout the lifetime of the same app-server, including several bursts of exactly 11 processes.

Examples from the creation timeline:

```text
2026-10-06 21:03    11
2026-10-06 21:06    11
2026-10-06 21:48    11
2026-10-06 22:35    11
```

The helpers were not simply the fixed startup cost of Codex.

## Clean restart comparison

After fully exiting Codex Desktop:

- the Codex app-server disappeared
- Codex-owned node_repl/code-mode helpers disappeared
- Windows committed memory dropped from 63.06 GB to 41.44 GB
- this released approximately 21.62 GB of system commit

After starting Codex Desktop again, the clean baseline was only:

```text
CodexNodeCount: 8
```

With three Codex sessions actively executing tasks, the process tree became:

```text
NodeTotal          : 44
MCP                : 24
CUA                : 12
NodeRepl           : 8
NodePrivateGB      : 2.54
CodexTreePrivateGB : 3.30
```

No additional visible Codex session was started.

Approximately 10 minutes later, while the same three sessions were still running:

```text
NodeTotal          : 55
MCP                : 30
CUA                : 15
NodeRepl           : 10
NodePrivateGB      : 3.18
CodexTreePrivateGB : 4.00
```

The increment was exactly:

```text
+6 MCP
+3 CUA
+2 node_repl
= +11 processes
```

This looks like another complete local runtime/helper batch being created while previous batches remain resident.

## System impact

The machine has approximately 32 GB physical RAM.

Before cleanup, under the full workload, I measured:

```text
CPU average                : 70.73%
CPU maximum                : 100%
Available memory minimum   : 494 MB
Committed memory           : 87–90%
Pages/sec average          : 6585.5
Page Reads/sec average     : 918.7
```

Windows was under severe paging pressure.

Docker was initially also running and amplified the memory pressure, so I stopped Docker.

After Docker was stopped, system pressure improved substantially, but the Codex helper accumulation still reproduced:

```text
Clean Codex start: 8 Node-family helpers
3 active sessions: 44 helpers
~10 minutes later: 55 helpers
```

Therefore Docker is not required to reproduce the Codex process accumulation.

There is no single application error dialog or explicit Codex error message. The observable failure is progressive helper-process accumulation, increasing committed/private memory, heavy paging, and severe degradation of Codex task throughput.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Fully exit Codex Desktop.

2. Verify that the previous Codex app-server and its node_repl/code-mode helper tree have exited.

3. Start Codex Desktop again.

4. Immediately inspect the Codex app-server descendant processes. On my machine, a clean startup has approximately:

```text
NodeTotal: 8
```

5. Start several normal Codex sessions. In my reproduction I used three concurrently active sessions.

The tasks were normal software-development/agent tasks involving local tools. Reasoning effort was generally Low or Medium; Fast mode was not enabled.

6. Periodically inspect the `codex.exe app-server` descendant process tree.

For example, the following PowerShell script counts the Node-family descendants and classifies them without printing complete command lines:

```powershell
$all = Get-CimInstance Win32_Process

$root = $all |
    Where-Object {
        $_.Name -eq "codex.exe" -and
        $_.CommandLine -match "app-server"
    } |
    Select-Object -First 1

if (-not $root) {
    throw "Codex app-server not found"
}

$rootId = [int]$root.ProcessId

$desc = New-Object 'System.Collections.Generic.HashSet[int]'
$null = $desc.Add($rootId)

$changed = $true

while ($changed) {
    $changed = $false

    foreach ($proc in $all) {
        $childProcessId  = [int]$proc.ProcessId
        $parentProcessId = [int]$proc.ParentProcessId

        if (
            $desc.Contains($parentProcessId) -and
            -not $desc.Contains($childProcessId)
        ) {
            $null = $desc.Add($childProcessId)
            $changed = $true
        }
    }
}

$nodes = $all |
    Where-Object {
        $_.Name -in @("node.exe", "node_repl.exe") -and
        $desc.Contains([int]$_.ProcessId)
    }

$runtime = @{}

Get-Process -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    ForEach-Object {
        $runtime[$_.Id] = $_
    }

$rows = foreach ($proc in $nodes) {
    $text = "$($proc.ExecutablePath) $($proc.CommandLine)"

    $category =
        if ($proc.Name -eq "node_repl.exe") {
            "node_repl"
        }
        elseif ($text -match "cua_node") {
            "CUA"
        }
        elseif ($text -match "mcp") {
            "MCP"
        }
        else {
            "Other"
        }

    $processId = [int]$proc.ProcessId
    $rp = $runtime[$processId]

    [pscustomobject]@{
        Category = $category
        PrivateMB = if ($rp) {
            [math]::Round($rp.PrivateMemorySize64 / 1MB, 1)
        }
        else {
            0
        }
    }
}

$rows |
    Group-Object Category |
    ForEach-Object {
        [pscustomobject]@{
            Category = $_.Name
            Count = $_.Count
            PrivateGB = [math]::Round(
                (($_.Group | Measure-Object PrivateMB -Sum).Sum / 1024),
                2
            )
        }
    } |
    Format-Table -AutoSize

"Total Node-family processes: $($nodes.Count)"
```

7. With three active sessions, I observed:

```text
NodeTotal: 44
MCP:       24
CUA:       12
node_repl:  8
```

8. Approximately 10 minutes later, without starting another visible session:

```text
NodeTotal: 55
MCP:       30
CUA:       15
node_repl: 10
```

This is an additional complete batch of:

```text
6 MCP + 3 CUA + 2 node_repl = 11 processes
```

9. During a longer app-server lifetime, allow normal Codex work to continue. In my earlier run the same app-server eventually reached approximately 200 Codex-owned Node-family processes and ~11.6 GB of Node private memory.

10. Fully exit Codex Desktop.

The accumulated Codex helper tree is cleared and system committed memory drops substantially.

11. Reopen Codex Desktop.

The process count returns to the clean baseline (approximately 8 on my machine), and then begins growing again as tasks execute.

## Session/context information

This problem was observed across several concurrent Codex sessions rather than one specific prompt.

- Concurrent visible sessions during the clean reproduction: 3
- Reasoning effort: normally Low or Medium, rarely High
- Fast mode: normally disabled
- The issue appears related to local runtime/helper lifecycle rather than a specific model response or prompt
- Session IDs are not included in this public issue, but I can provide relevant thread/session identifiers privately if maintainers need them


### What is the expected behavior?

Codex Desktop should keep the number of local MCP/CUA/node_repl helper processes bounded.

A new task, tool turn, subagent, or runtime context should not indefinitely add another complete local helper/MCP process batch.

When a runtime is no longer needed, its local stdio MCP/CUA/node_repl process tree should be terminated or safely reused.

Long-running Codex Desktop usage with several sessions should not require periodically restarting the entire application to recover tens of gigabytes of committed memory.

The expected behavior is:

- bounded helper-process count
- reuse or teardown of obsolete runtime/MCP process pools
- stable private/committed memory over long-running sessions
- no progressive Windows paging or system-wide slowdown caused by retained Codex helper processes

### Additional information

## Codex app-server configuration

The affected Codex Desktop app-server was launched with this general command shape:

```text
codex.exe
-c features.code_mode_host=true
app-server
--analytics-default-enabled
-c features.prefer_mxc=true
-c plugins.codex-app-tools@openai-bundled.mcp_servers.codex_app.enabled=true
-c plugins.code-review@openai-bundled.mcp_servers.code-review.enabled=true
```

No credentials or private project information are included above.

## Hardware

- approximately 32 GB physical RAM
- DDR5-5600
- Windows x64
- Docker was stopped during the clean reproduction described above

## Important A/B observation

Before fully exiting Codex:

```text
CommittedGB: 63.06
```

After fully exiting Codex:

```text
CommittedGB: 41.44
```

Difference:

```text
~21.62 GB system commit released
```

After restarting Codex:

```text
Initial Codex Node-family helper count: 8
```

The helper count then increased again as normal Codex work continued.

This makes the condition highly reproducible and strongly tied to the lifetime of the Codex Desktop app-server/process tree rather than permanent OS memory usage.

## Possibly related existing reports

This may be related to the same Windows MCP/helper lifecycle problem reported in:

- #40579
- #32797
- #33531
- #26327

I am filing this separately because the issue is still reproducible on the much newer Codex Desktop version `26.1002.6548.0`, and I have a clean restart baseline plus process-count/memory measurements showing the progression from 8 -> 44 -> 55 -> approximately 200 helpers during longer-running usage.

## Exact error

```
Computer Use has been stopped for this turn because it could not determine the current browser URL on Windows with enough confidence to enforce policy. Stop your work and send a final message noting why Computer Use ended.
```

Automation stopped after this error; URL verification was not bypassed.

- No supported local fix was established. Browser/security settings were not changed; no reinstall or downgrade was performed.

## Related reports and requested action

Related: #43880 and #46943. These are symptom matches, not proof of the same root cause. #46943 may be related to the affected user's prior investigation; its authorship was not verified.

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using?

- Codex desktop app: **26.1002.52244**, build **13536**, production channel
- Bundled CLI: **codex-cli 0.162.0-alpha.2**
- App update check reports **up to date**
- Observed: **October 7, 2026 (UTC+08:00)**

### What platform is your computer?

- macOS 26.6 (25G72)
- Apple Silicon / arm64

### What issue are you seeing?

After the recent desktop app update, the agent repeatedly triggered interactive command approval for operations that were already explicitly and persistently authorized by the user's project instructions, and in one case already matched an approved command prefix.

This report is about the agent/tool-approval integration choosing `sandbox_permissions=require_escalated` unnecessarily. The user did not independently request the popup: the assistant generated the escalation request.

The project instructions explicitly stated all of the following:

- Routine Git operations, including `fetch`, `pull`, `push`, branch/worktree management, are continuously authorized.
- Read-only diagnostics are continuously authorized.
- Exact task-owned directories under `/tmp` and `/private/tmp` may be cleaned up without another confirmation after path, size, and ownership are checked.
- Running a shell command or running outside the sandbox is not by itself a reason to ask for approval.
- If an operation is already authorized, the agent must not add a synonymous conversational confirmation.

A saved command prefix also already allowed `git fetch`.

Despite that context, the agent did the following:

1. Combined `git fetch --prune origin` with read-only `git status`, `git rev-parse`, and document reads.
2. Explicitly set `sandbox_permissions=require_escalated` and supplied a user-facing approval justification.
3. The desktop app displayed an approval prompt.
4. After the user objected, the same `git fetch --prune origin` was run normally without `require_escalated` and succeeded immediately.

A second occurrence involved cleanup:

1. The agent created a uniquely named task directory under `/private/tmp`.
2. It read back the exact path, ownership, and size (574 MB), satisfying the user's cleanup policy.
3. The agent still used `require_escalated` for `rm -rf <exact-task-directory>`, causing another approval prompt.
4. After the user objected, an exact-path `find <same-directory> -depth -delete` command ran without an approval prompt and removed the directory successfully.

The assistant then inaccurately told the user that the platform had "misclassified" the already-authorized command. Inspection of the assistant's own tool call showed that the assistant itself had selected `require_escalated`. The assistant later corrected this statement.

The user reports that this behavior appeared after the desktop app upgrade. That is a timing correlation, not proof that build 26.1002.52244 introduced the root cause.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

items.body:
# Windows sandbox provisioning fails with os error 32 when any runtime file is in use (regression in the 0.162.0-alpha.2 helper)

## Summary

On Windows, `codex-windows-sandbox-setup.exe` aborts provisioning with
`helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors` whenever any file in the
`cua_node` runtime tree is currently open by a running process. The desktop app
keeps `codex-computer-use-swift.exe` and the node MCP hosts running from that
same tree, so from the moment the app is up every sandboxed command is rejected.

The step that fails (`runtime read/execute validation`) does not exist in older
helpers; it appears together with the helper shipped in build
`0.162.0-alpha.2`.

## Environment

- Codex desktop app: `OpenAI.Codex` 26.1002.6548.0 (MSIX), Windows x86_64, zh-CN
- CLI / sandbox helper: `0.162.0-alpha.2`, binary dir `979a96ce184041d1`
- Config: `[windows] sandbox = "elevated"`
- Sandbox accounts: `CodexSandboxOffline`, `CodexSandboxOnline` (group `CodexSandboxUsers`)

## Symptom

- `codex doctor --summary` reports:
  `✗ sandbox  elevated Windows sandbox provisioning recorded a structured failure`
- Any sandboxed command fails with:
  `windows sandbox failed: helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors`
- `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\.sandbox\setup_error.json` contains:
  `{"code": "helper_unknown_error", "message": "setup refresh had errors"}`

## Root cause / evidence

From `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\.sandbox\sandbox.<date>.log`:

```
START: cmd /c echo SANDBOX_OK
setup refresh: spawning ...\codex-windows-sandbox-setup.exe (cwd=..., payload_len=5160)
failed to grant non-inheriting read-attributes ACE on user profile C:\Users\<user>:
  open ACL target for root-only update: <another process is using this file> (os error 32); continuing setup
runtime read/execute validation failed: validate runtime read/execute access on
  C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\OpenAI\Codex\runtimes\cua_node\<hash>\bin\node_repl.exe:
  open ACL target for root-only update: <another process is using this file> (os error 32)
setup refresh completed with errors: [...]
setup error: setup refresh had errors
```

- `os error 32` = `ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION`.
- Ending every `node_repl.exe` process does not help: the failure simply moves to
  the next in-use file, e.g.
  `...\runtimes\cua_node\<hash>\bin\node_modules\@oai\sky\bin\windows\swift\x64\VCRUNTIME140_1.dll`.
- The app immediately respawns the holder: `codex-computer-use-swift.exe` was
  recreated within ~0.4 s of being stopped, and the refresh failed again on the
  same DLL. So a quiescent runtime tree cannot be reached while the app runs.
- Pre-granting permissions does not help. Explicit `(RX)` ACEs for
  `CodexSandboxUsers`, `CodexSandboxOffline` and `CodexSandboxOnline` were applied
  recursively to the whole runtime tree (2702 files, `icacls ... /T`), and the
  failure was byte-for-byte identical. Helper-managed files
  (e.g. `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\.sandbox-bin\codex.exe`) also carry only
  inherited ACEs, so the validation is not about the resulting ACE shape - it is
  about being able to open the target at all.

## Regression evidence

Occurrences of `runtime read/execute` in the sandbox logs on the same machine
with the same configuration:

| Date | Helper build in use | `runtime read/execute` occurrences |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2026-09-29 | `faa963e871dd422c` | 0 |
| 2026-09-30 | `c6fe824d725f02d7` / `ca9abb0b4d8ac692` | 0 |
| 2026-10-02 | `c6fe824d725f02d7` | 0 |
| 2026-10-05 | `be3fd7e5c1969ff6` | 0 |
| 2026-10-07 | `979a96ce184041d1` (new) | 156 |

The step appears only with the new helper. On 2026-10-07 the new runtime
directory was materialized at 14:56:08 and the first failure occurred at
14:57:44, i.e. 96 seconds later. Before that the sandbox had worked continuously
for a week.

## Suggested fix

- Tolerate `ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION` (os error 32) for the runtime ACL step the
  same way the profile-ACE step already does (it logs `continuing setup` instead
  of failing). Skip in-use files rather than failing the whole provisioning.
- Or validate runtime access read-only (`AccessCheck`, or compare the effective
  ACEs) instead of opening the target for an ACL update.
- Or defer the runtime validation until no process is running from the runtime
  tree, and cache the result so it is not re-attempted on every command.

## Impact

The Windows sandbox is unusable whenever the desktop app is running, which is
always during normal use. Running commands escalated/unsandboxed is the only
workaround, and that can itself be refused by a granular approval policy
(`you cannot ask for escalated permissions if the approval policy is Granular(...)`).

## Additional impact: Computer Use / Browser automation is blocked as well

The same provisioning failure also prevents the `node_repl` kernel from
starting, which takes down the whole automation stack built on it (Browser
plugin, Computer Use, unified-computer-use). A `cua_repl` call fails with:

```
node_repl kernel exited unexpectedly
node_repl diagnostics: {"kernel_pid":...,"kernel_status":"exited(code=1)",
  "kernel_stderr_tail":"windows sandbox failed: helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors",
  "reason":"stdout_eof","stream_error":null}
```

So the regression is not limited to shell command execution: it also disables
browser and desktop automation features, because their runtime kernel is
launched through the same sandbox provisioning path.

The steps above describe the configuration/session scenario for maintainers to reproduce; the attached recorded timeline is the directly observed case.

#### Small read-only evidence collector

This prints only the relevant connector flags and skill identifiers, not the full configuration or full prompt. Run it in the affected agent environment with `CODEX_HOME` and `CODEX_THREAD_ID` set, using Python 3.11+:

```python

import os
import re
import tomllib
from pathlib import Path

home = Path(os.environ["CODEX_HOME"])
thread_id = os.environ["CODEX_THREAD_ID"]
config = tomllib.loads((home / "config.toml").read_text())

for connector in (
    "connector_20205bf7d4e99a89d7154bb849718324",
    "connector_openai_chatgpt_pets",
):
    print(connector, config.get("apps", {}).get(connector, {}).get("enabled"))

for rollout in (home / "sessions").rglob(f"*{thread_id}*.jsonl"):
    for line in rollout.open():
        item = json.loads(line)
        payload = item.get("payload", {})
        if item.get("type") == "session_meta":
            print("runtime", payload.get("cli_version"))
        if payload.get("type") != "message" or payload.get("role") != "developer":
            continue
        text = "\n".join(
            part.get("text", "") for part in payload.get("content", [])
            if isinstance(part, dict)
        )
        if "### Available skills" in text:
            names = re.findall(r"^- ((?:sites|work-pets):[^: \n]+):", text, re.M)
            print("catalogue_timestamp", item.get("timestamp"))
            print("affected_skills", names)
```

### What is the expected behavior?

Disabling an integration should give users a clear, persistent way to prevent that integration from shaping the agent's workflow.

For plugins whose `.app.json` declares an app as `required: true`, please either:

- Suppress their dependent skills from the actionable model-visible catalogue when that required app is disabled; or
- Make the separate plugin/connector/skill enablement states explicit in the UI and runtime catalogue, mark dependent skills unavailable, and provide a supported per-plugin opt-out that removes their instructions from new sessions.

The agent should not be encouraged to select a workflow whose required native capability has been disabled.

### Additional information

#### Scope and diagnostic qualifications

- No evidence of disabled-tool execution, authentication bypass, deployment, or data access through Sites/Pets was observed. Their native tools were absent from this session's exposed tool inventory.
- Cache retention alone is not treated as a defect or as proof of activation. The evidence is the skill catalogue in the recorded session and the subsequent Sites skill read.
- The verified setting is [`apps.<id>.enabled`](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-reference), which the configuration reference describes as controlling an app/connector. Please clarify whether retaining skills from plugins with a disabled **required** connector is intentional and, if so, how the user can reliably opt out of both parts.
- Usernames, private project details, complete prompts, credentials, and unrelated configuration were omitted. The excerpted connector/plugin identifiers are the shipped integration identifiers.

#### Doctor summary

items.title: [Windows][Desktop][IAB] ChatGPT page falls into Cloudflare / signed-out state after a few minutes and recovers immediately on refresh

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app

items.body:
## Summary

On Codex Desktop for Windows, a logged-in `chatgpt.com` page opened inside the built-in in-app browser (IAB) repeatedly falls into a Cloudflare / apparently unauthenticated state after a short period of time, usually within roughly 1–10 minutes.

A normal manual page refresh immediately restores the already-authenticated ChatGPT session. No username/password or OAuth login is required again.

The same ChatGPT account remains logged in normally in regular Chrome/Edge sessions. The problem has only been observed in the Codex built-in browser.

Local read-only diagnostics found frequent IAB route/lifecycle errors during the same Desktop process lifetime, including:

```text
No ChatGPT browser route is available
renderer disposed
browser sidebar guest torn down
```

However, the available logs do not contain direct `403`, `401`, `cf-mitigated`, `challenge`, or `auth.openai.com` entries, so the current evidence does not establish whether Cloudflare itself is the root cause.

The strongest local evidence currently points to an IAB route/WebContents/session lifecycle problem that may leave the visible page in a stale browser state until navigation is reinitialized by refresh.

## Environment

- OS: Windows x64
- Codex Desktop MSIX package: `26.930.7945.0`
- Bundled Browser plugin: `26.930.61225`
- Chromium components:
  - `ChatGPT.exe`: `154.0.8037.98`
  - `chrome.dll`: `154.0.8037.98`
- Browser backend: built-in IAB
- Desktop process remained continuously running while the issue reproduced
- Browser plugin is enabled
- No custom IAB partition/network configuration was found in `config.toml`

There are two separate Codex CLI installations on the machine (`0.150.1` and `0.160.1`), but there is currently no evidence connecting this CLI difference to the IAB symptom.

## Reproduction

1. Launch Codex Desktop on Windows.
2. Open the built-in browser.
3. Navigate to `https://chatgpt.com/`.
4. Log in normally.
5. Leave/use the page for several minutes.
6. After a short interval, typically approximately 1–10 minutes, the page can enter a Cloudflare / apparently signed-out state.
7. Manually refresh the current page.
8. ChatGPT immediately returns to the authenticated state without requiring login again.

This behavior has occurred repeatedly.

Regular Chrome/Edge sessions using the same account do not reproduce the problem.

## Actual behavior

The visible IAB page loses its usable authenticated state after a short period and displays a Cloudflare / unauthenticated-looking state.

A simple refresh restores the existing login immediately.

This suggests that persistent authentication data may still be present, while some transient browser/session/network state has become stale.

## Expected behavior

An authenticated ChatGPT page opened in the Codex built-in browser should remain usable for the normal lifetime of the session.

If the underlying IAB route, renderer, guest WebContents, or browser session is replaced or disposed, the visible page should be rebound correctly or recover automatically rather than entering a stale Cloudflare/authentication state that requires manual refresh.

## Local read-only diagnostics

The active Codex Desktop process was not restarted during the diagnostic period.

The Desktop user-data directory contains separate Chromium cookie stores for the default profile and the IAB partition, including paths corresponding to:

```text
Default/Cookies
Default/Partitions/codex-browser-app/Cookies
```

Both databases showed current-day writes.

Cookie contents were not read because the active database was locked by the running application. No attempt was made to bypass the lock, decrypt cookies, or inspect credential values.

Therefore, the diagnostic does **not** establish whether `cf_clearance` or another specific cookie is present, absent, expired, or different between partitions.

### Desktop log observations

During one day of use:

- `No ChatGPT browser route is available` appeared **186 times**.
- The failures clustered in several periods, including approximately:
  - 14:55–15:02
  - 15:47–15:50
  - 16:03–16:12
  - 16:33–16:42
- `renderer disposed` appeared 5 times.
- `browser sidebar guest torn down` appeared 5 times.
- Embedded-page process IDs changed across lifecycle events while the containing window ID remained unchanged.
- No matching log entries containing the following strings were found:
  - `401`
  - `403`
  - `Cloudflare`
  - `challenge`
  - `cf-mitigated`
  - `auth.openai.com`
- One `ERR_NETWORK_CHANGED` event occurred much earlier and did not align with most later IAB route-error periods.

These observations support repeated IAB route / embedded-page lifecycle changes, but they do not by themselves prove that those events caused the visible Cloudflare page.

## Current hypothesis

The current working hypothesis is:

```text
IAB page is authenticated and working
    ↓
IAB route / guest WebContents / renderer lifecycle changes
    ↓
visible page remains present but part of its browser/session state becomes stale
    ↓
ChatGPT / Cloudflare-facing navigation or request state becomes unusable
    ↓
user refreshes the page
    ↓
navigation/session initialization runs again
    ↓
existing authenticated ChatGPT session works again
```

This is a hypothesis based on temporal and architectural evidence, not a confirmed root cause.

## Troubleshooting / controls

The following conditions make a general account/login problem less likely:

- The same ChatGPT account remains logged in normally in regular browsers.
- No cookies or site data were intentionally cleared.
- No logout was performed.
- Refresh alone restores the session.
- No relevant custom network/IAB configuration was found.
- The Browser plugin version on disk matches the configured plugin version.
- The Desktop process itself remained alive during the observed lifecycle events.

No cache deletion, cookie deletion, profile reset, registry modification, Codex reinstall, or Windows network modification was performed during diagnostics.

## Related reports

Possibly related:

- #48670 — Windows built-in browser route can disappear / route window not live
- #48360 — Windows IAB page reads time out and browser session route is lost
- #43210 — replacement IAB backend/route can be disposed during lifecycle transitions

This report differs in its primary user-visible symptom: an already logged-in `chatgpt.com` page becomes Cloudflare / unauthenticated-looking after a few minutes and immediately recovers after a normal refresh.

## Request

Could the Codex Desktop team investigate whether:

1. IAB route replacement or guest WebContents teardown can leave the visible page bound to stale browser/session state;
2. the `codex-browser-app` Chromium partition is recreated or rebound during these lifecycle events;
3. transient network/session state required by `chatgpt.com` / Cloudflare is lost while persistent authentication cookies remain available;
4. a stale IAB page can be automatically rebound/reloaded when its route or browser host is replaced;
5. additional lifecycle logging could associate the visible WebContents, browser session, route, partition, and renderer across teardown/recreation events.

I can provide sanitized timestamps or targeted log excerpts if maintainers need them. Raw cookies, tokens, account identifiers, conversation IDs, and private browsing data have intentionally been omitted.

A nontechnical user working across two Windows PCs lost development time trying to determine which computer a continued chat and Computer Use were actually connected to. - The user manually copies packaged builds to a secondary PC for testing.
- This chat continued from a referenced ChatGPT conversation about launching a packaged build on the secondary PC.

This is an observed workflow failure, not a confirmed backend routing defect. We have not verified that opening the chat on another device automatically changes its execution host, nor independently inspected what device indicators or selectors the user could see. The exact desktop app version was not collected. The Computer Use skill used was bundled version 26.930.41038.

## Expected experience / requested improvements

1. Persistently display the actual validated execution computer for each chat, separately from conversation sync/backing, project location, and the device displaying the chat.
2. Show which computer each capability targets, especially filesystem access and Computer Use, and whether it is connected and usable.
3. Provide a clear, discoverable way to move or reconnect an existing chat to another authorized computer while preserving context. Explain any limitations with a concrete next step.
4. When continuing a referenced conversation, make clear whether only its conversation context is carried over or also its execution environment.
5. Detect a mismatch between the user's requested computer and the effective executor before promising to edit a project or searching the wrong device. The assistant should verify identity and provide actionable guidance rather than generic instructions to reconnect.

A connected/disconnected label alone does not tell the user whether the intended computer, files, project and tools are available. This ambiguity is a major productivity obstacle for general users, not just a terminology issue.

We need a documented way for an authorized local client to send additional input into a turn already running in the ChatGPT desktop app, without starting another turn or another driver.

## Environment and observed behavior

- macOS; the inspected desktop installation bundles Codex CLI 0.160.1. The desktop app's own marketing/build version was not recorded. This is an installed-version observation, not a claim about the latest release.
- During active work in an existing desktop chat, an external `codex queue` message remained queued behind the active turn. Manually choosing **Steer** incorporated it into that active turn. The native in-app messaging surface also separately showed active-turn incorporation.
- The bundled CLI's complete queue help and top-level help expose no external steer option or subcommand in the inspected version.
- The inspected app-owned server was started over stdio without `--listen`. Process/socket inspection found no named Unix listening endpoint or local TCP listener for that server. This is a bounded observation, not proof that no undisclosed interface exists.

These are observations from an existing installation. We have not run a new clean-install reproduction or a shared-daemon migration.

## Observed sequence

1. A desktop chat has an active turn.
2. An authorized external local sender queues a short text message for that existing chat.
3. The message stays queued behind active work.
4. The user chooses **Steer** in the desktop app; the message becomes part of the same active turn.

For local integrations, we would like the equivalent of step 4 through a supported interface, with an explicit active-turn precondition.

## Requested interface or guidance

The [App Server documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/app-server#steer-an-active-turn) describes `turn/steer` with `threadId`, `expectedTurnId` and `input`, returning `turnId`; it rejects a missing or mismatched active turn. The unresolved integration question is how an external authorized client connects to the server already owning the desktop turn. The protocol method alone does not establish that connection.

Please identify an existing supported command/attachment contract, or consider exposing one that:

- Identifies the current Desktop-owned thread and active turn without creating, resuming or taking over another driver.
- Defines local client authorization, connection lifetime and permission scope.
- Sends input only when `expectedTurnId` still matches the active turn and returns the accepted turn identity.
- Rejects idle/stale/mismatched requests clearly, so an uncertain result is not blindly retried or duplicated through a queue fallback.
- Provides acceptance/event guidance so transport acceptance and subsequent incorporation can be checked separately.

We are not requesting credential extraction, stdio interception, an unauthenticated listener or a restart of active work. No local-daemon, listener or settings change was made for this report. Until a supported route is established, manual Steer remains the workaround.

This report contains no local paths, actual thread/turn identifiers, personal or internal desk names, message transcripts, credentials, screenshots or log attachments.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: app

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From "About Codex" dialog)?

26.1002.6548.0 (bundled `codex-cli 0.162.0-alpha.2`). The issue started right after the auto-update from 26.930.

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT account

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 Pro, build 26200, x64. `[windows] sandbox = "elevated"`.

### What issue are you seeing?

Related: #51590 (same symptom). This issue adds a root cause in `windows-sandbox-rs` and a tested fix.

Every sandboxed local command fails before process creation:

```
exec_command failed: CreateProcess { message: "Rejected(\"Failed to create unified exec process: helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors\")" }
```

The sandbox log shows:

```
runtime read/execute validation failed: validate runtime read/execute access on
%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\runtimes\cua_node\<hash>\bin\node_modules\@oai\sky\bin\windows\swift\x64\VCRUNTIME140_1.dll:
open ACL target for root-only update: The process cannot access the file because
it is being used by another process. (os error 32)
```

The same error appears for `node.exe` and `node_repl.exe` in the runtime. It also appears, non-fatally, for the user profile root (`failed to grant non-inheriting read-attributes ACE on user profile`).

**Root cause.** `ensure_allow_mask_aces_with_inheritance_impl` in `codex-rs/windows-sandbox-rs/src/acl.rs` opens root-only (non-inheriting) targets with `MAXIMUM_ALLOWED` before it checks whether an update is needed. This came in with #49690. For the file owner, that handle includes write access. Windows rejects write access to an image that a running process has loaded, so the open fails with `ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION`. The app's own computer-use helpers (`codex-computer-use-swift.exe`, `node.exe`, `node_repl.exe`) keep these runtime files loaded, and the app restarts the Swift helper within milliseconds of a kill. Restarting the app does not help.

The ACL was already correct. The sandbox group already had inherited access, so no ACE needed to be written. With the app fully closed, the same setup refresh succeeds with `errors=[]` and leaves every runtime ACL unchanged.

A direct `CreateFileW` check against the loaded DLL:

| Access mask | Result |
|---|---|
| `MAXIMUM_ALLOWED` | error 32 |
| `READ_CONTROL \| WRITE_DAC` | success |

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Use Codex App 26.1002 on Windows with the elevated sandbox, with computer use enabled so the runtime helpers are running.
2. Run any command in a sandboxed permission mode, or run `codex sandbox -P :workspace -- cmd /c dir` with the bundled CLI while the app is open.
3. The command fails with `helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors`.

### What is the expected behavior?

When the ACL is already correct, setup refresh should not need write access to runtime files, and commands should run.

### Additional information

**Proposed fix (tested):** https://github.com/erson/codex/commit/2bd3cd554dd26b40078265df121ca7546981bb58

- Read the DACL through `fetch_dacl_handle` (a `READ_CONTROL` handle) for both root-only and inheriting grants.
- Open the `MAXIMUM_ALLOWED` handle only when at least one ACE must be written. That keeps the no-propagation behavior from #49690.
- Add the regression test `noninheriting_grant_skips_open_for_write_when_ace_is_present`. It holds a read-only-sharing handle on the target, like a loaded image, and checks that an up-to-date root-only grant succeeds.

I tried to open a pull request, but the repository does not accept external PRs, so the commit is linked here instead.

**Testing.** The computer-use helper held the runtime files during all end-to-end runs. The baseline was the released 0.162.0-alpha.2.

- **Unit:** the new test fails on `main` with the same `open ACL target for root-only update … (os error 32)` error and passes with the fix. `noninheriting_read_attributes_preserve_unprotected_child_dacl` still passes. Across `cargo test -p codex-windows-sandbox`, the set of failing tests is identical with and without the fix, apart from the new test. The remaining failures on this machine are environment-specific (junction and live-sandbox tests). Clippy is clean.
- **`codex sandbox -P :workspace`:** `cmd` read and write, `powershell.exe` write and read, `pwsh.exe` write and read. Baseline: 4/4 fail with `setup refresh had errors`. Fix: 4/4 succeed, and setup refresh logs `errors=[]`.
- **Agent turn:** `codex exec -s workspace-write -c windows.sandbox="elevated" -c features.prefer_mxc=false`, with the same model on both builds. Baseline: the error above, and no file is written. Fix: setup refresh logs `errors=[]`, and the agent writes and reads back a probe file.

**Limits.**

items.title: Linux: codex-linux-sandbox leftovers reparented to systemd --user after session end / terminate

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
## Summary

On Linux, after a Codex app-server session ends (or after protocol APIs report that a background terminal was terminated), `codex-linux-sandbox` process trees are often **reparented to the user's `systemd --user` instance** and keep running indefinitely. They accumulate across sessions and consume CPU/memory until manually cleaned up.

This looks related to broader orphan-process reports such as #15379 and #47735, but the Linux-specific signature here is: **argv0/`codex-linux-sandbox` wrappers whose PPID becomes `systemd --user` (not the live app-server)**.

## Environment (this machine, 2026-10-07)

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| OS | Linux 7.0.0-31-generic |
| User session | `systemd --user` present (adopts orphaned children) |
| systemd | 259 (259.5-0ubuntu3.4) |
| codex-cli (current) | 0.159.2 |
| Earlier spike | codex-cli 0.155.1 (2026-09-26) |
| Sandbox | `codex-linux-sandbox` (often under bwrap) |

## Impact observed

On one long-lived Linux workstation we measured:

- **~75** leftover `codex-linux-sandbox` processes at once
- **Oldest age ~138–141 hours** (~5.7–5.9 days)
- All had **PPID = `systemd --user`**, none were still under a live `codex app-server` tree
- Children were mostly stuck `uv`/`pytest`/`zsh` leftovers from finished agent turns

We only performed **read-only detection** for diagnosis; cleanup was a separate, explicit, PID-precise local action (not the default product behavior).

## Minimal reproduction (app-server process tree)

Use a marked no-op command (e.g. `sleep` + unique suffix) in an empty temp cwd. Confirm the marker is absent before starting. Avoid concurrent `codex exec` noise.

1. Start `codex app-server --listen stdio://`. Open a turn that runs the marked command in the read-only/managed sandbox and accept the approval.
2. **Scenario A — `turn/interrupt`**: record the protocol ack, then inspect the process tree immediately and again ~10s later (PID, PPID, command, parent name).
3. **Scenario B — `thread/backgroundTerminals/terminate`**: start another marked command, call terminate, record the ack, inspect immediately and ~10s later.
4. **Scenario C — app-server exit**: start another marked command, close app-server stdin so it exits, record exit code, inspect immediately and ~10s later.
5. In each case, note whether the parent is still `codex` / app-server, or has become the user's `systemd --user` (or PID 1).

### Expected

- **Scenario A**: If “unified exec may keep running after interrupt” is intentional, the command may still be alive, but its parent should remain that app-server instance—not init/`systemd --user`.
- **Scenarios B and C**: After the protocol reports termination / the app-server has exited, the marked command and its `bwrap` / `codex-linux-sandbox` ancestors should exit. No same-marker leftovers should remain.

### Actual (2026-09-26 spike, codex-cli 0.155.1)

| Scenario | Protocol | ~10s later |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `turn/interrupt` | `turn/completed(status=interrupted)` in a few ms; thread `idle` | Sandbox command still running while app-server still alive |
| `thread/backgroundTerminals/terminate` | `{"terminated": true}` | `bwrap` gone; `codex-linux-sandbox → …` **reparented to `systemd --user` and still running** |
| app-server exit (stdin EOF) | exit code 0 | Entire command tree **reparented to `systemd --user` and still running** |

Note: Codex's own `<turn_aborted>` text mentions that the unified exec process may keep running after interrupt, so scenario A may be by design. **B and C look like a lifecycle bug**: protocol/process exit already signaled, yet the sandbox tree survives under `systemd --user`.

## Request

1. On session end / successful `backgroundTerminals/terminate` / app-server shutdown, **reap the associated `codex-linux-sandbox` (and descendants)** instead of leaving them for `systemd --user` to adopt.
2. If intentional keep-alive exists for interrupt, document it clearly and provide an **official cleanup / lifecycle guarantee** for Linux (when processes are expected to die vs. when operators must clean them up).
3. Optionally expose a supported way to list/reap stale sandbox trees so hosts do not need ad-hoc `kill` by name.

## Community note (detection only)

A third-party read-only scanner for this Linux signature lives in https://github.com/zleo-ai/vyane/pull/1280 (`vyane liveness sandbox-orphans`). It only reads `/proc` and does **not** send signals. Sharing it as ambient context for maintainers—not a request to adopt that code.

## Related

- #15379 Orphaned child processes persist after Codex parent exits (macOS / general)
- #47735 Short-lived `codex app-server` processes orphan marketplace clones

items.body:
## Summary

After the October 7 update, the Windows app repeatedly failed to complete Windows setup and blocked sandboxed command execution. Initially I also could not change the chat's permission mode normally. A local recovery restored the UI, but actual elevated sandbox execution still failed, including after rebooting Windows.

This report adds controlled Win32 access-mask measurements and a tested, reversible local workaround to the existing reports. It is not a claim that this bug first appeared on October 7 or affects every installation.

## Environment

- Windows 11 Home, 24H2, build 26100.4946, x64.
- Desktop package version reported by `codex doctor`: `26.1002.6548.0`.
- App update checker reported `26.1002.51308`, build `13417`, production channel, up to date.
- Bundled core: `codex-cli 0.162.0-alpha.2`.
- Windows sandbox setting: `elevated`.
- Report and tests: October 7, 2026, Asia/Shanghai.
- Runtime: `cua_node/2c9e75c4e9c71beb`.

## Impact and frustration

I appreciate the new features and the pace of development. However, continuing to ship new features while recurring Windows sandbox failures interrupt basic development work is unacceptable for a development tool. Reliability is a core feature too.

Users should not have to spend hours collecting logs, restarting processes, rebooting Windows, and manually changing runtime file permissions just to restore command execution after an update. Please give these existing reliability problems, regression tests, and supported recovery procedures the same priority as new capabilities.

The related reports below have different details; I am not claiming they all have an identical root cause. They do show a recurring Windows sandbox reliability problem.

## Reproduction on this installation

1. Open Codex on Windows with its runtime processes running.
2. Select the elevated sandbox.
3. Run a harmless command through the bundled CLI, with an existing directory as the working directory:

```powershell
& "<bundled-core>\codex.exe" sandbox -C "<test-directory>" -P ':read-only' -c 'windows.sandbox="elevated"' 'C:\Windows\System32\whoami.exe'
```

4. The command fails before it starts:

```text
windows sandbox failed: helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors
```

5. The new sandbox log identifies the fatal error:

```text
runtime read/execute validation failed:
validate runtime read/execute access on
%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\runtimes\cua_node\<runtime>\bin\node_repl.exe:
open ACL target for root-only update:
The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process. (os error 32)
setup refresh completed with errors
```

The same error also occurred on loaded Microsoft runtime DLLs, including `VCRUNTIME140_1.dll`.

Rebooting Windows did not resolve this. The reboot was verified at 15:44, and a new attempt at 15:47 failed with the same error. An earlier, separate `helper_sandbox_lock_failed` on `.sandbox-bin` was recovered first; it should not be conflated with this subsequent sharing violation.

## Controlled diagnostic evidence

The sandbox group already had ReadAndExecute access to `node_repl.exe`. Using `CreateFileW` on the same active file, with identical sharing flags (`FILE_SHARE_READ | FILE_SHARE_WRITE | FILE_SHARE_DELETE`), `OPEN_EXISTING`, and `FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS`:

| Desired access | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `READ_CONTROL` | Success |
| `READ_CONTROL | WRITE_DAC` | Success |
| `MAXIMUM_ALLOWED` | Windows error 32 |

The same comparison produced the same results on the loaded `VCRUNTIME140_1.dll`.

I then temporarily added a non-inheriting deny ACE for the current user covering only `FILE_WRITE_DATA | FILE_APPEND_DATA` (mask `0x6`) on `node_repl.exe`. The `MAXIMUM_ALLOWED` open immediately succeeded. The original ACL was restored after this initial comparison.

## Source evidence and suspected cause

The published source for the matching core version contains the corresponding open:

[acl.rs at rust-v0.162.0-alpha.2, lines 548–556](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.0-alpha.2/codex-rs/windows-sandbox-rs/src/acl.rs#L548-L556)

`ensure_allow_mask_aces_with_inheritance_impl` uses `access_mode(MAXIMUM_ALLOWED)` for the root-only path and the exact error context shown in the log. Runtime validation calls the read/execute grant path for files.

The measurements strongly support unnecessary data-write access causing the sharing violation. I have not debugger- or hash-matched the installed helper binary to the published source, so the proposed source-level diagnosis still needs maintainer confirmation.

## Tested local recovery

After backing up the original security descriptors, I applied the same narrow, non-inheriting current-user deny ACE to six runtime files that produced sharing conflicts:

- `node_repl.exe`
- `node.exe`
- `codex-computer-use-swift.exe`
- `VCRUNTIME140_1.dll`
- `VCRUNTIME140.dll`
- `MSVCP140.dll`

Read, execute, and ACL-management access were retained; file contents were not modified. The configuration remained `elevated`.

Afterwards:

- `whoami` ran successfully under `<MACHINE>\CodexSandboxOffline`.
- Creating, reading, and deleting a file inside the allowed working directory succeeded.
- Writing a fresh test file outside that directory was denied; the host process could write to the same location.
- The bundled Node runtime executed inside the elevated sandbox.
- Direct external TCP access that worked from the host returned `EACCES` inside the sandbox. Local loopback remained reachable; this is not a claim of complete network isolation.
- `codex doctor` reported `sandbox.helpers.status=ok`, `backend=elevated`, and `provisioning=complete`.

This is a local workaround, not an upstream fix or a general recommendation. It can interfere with in-place runtime file updates, and replacement runtimes may require reapplication. Original ACL backups and a rollback script were preserved.

## Requested resolution

Please investigate using the minimum necessary handle access for live runtime files: inspect ACLs with read-security access and request ACL-write access only when necessary, while preserving deny entries, non-inheriting update semantics, and sandbox security checks.

Please add regression coverage for already-running EXEs and loaded DLLs, provide a supported recovery that preserves projects and chat history, and show the actual file and Win32 error in the setup UI.

Related reports: #51601, #51596, #50520, and #49025. This report adds the controlled access-mask comparison and measured recovery; other reporters' observations are not attributed to my machine.

Personal usernames, device names, SIDs, credentials, sandbox secrets, private project data, and full chat transcripts are omitted.

## Summary
Windows sandbox initialization fails when a Codex desktop chat has a writable workspace on a Google Drive for desktop G: path. Both shell and in-app browser automation fail before their actual operations begin. Removing the G: folders from the project's folder list and restarting the desktop app did not clear the failing path from the existing chat's sandbox setup.

## Environment
- Windows, PowerShell, Codex desktop app
- Bundled command-runner version observed in sandbox logs: 0.160.1 (desktop app version not collected)
- `[windows] sandbox = "elevated"`
- Google Drive for desktop mounted as G:, with a Unicode workspace path
- Observed on 2026-10-07, approximately 16:45–16:58 KST (UTC+09:00)
- Personal usernames, business folder names, account information and document contents omitted

## Steps observed
1. Start a desktop project/chat with a writable folder under `G:\<Google Drive folder>\<Unicode workspace>`.
2. Attempt shell execution or connect the browser automation tool to an already-open in-app browser tab.
3. Observe sandbox setup failure before the operation runs.
4. Change the project's folders to a local directory under `C:\Users\<user>\Documents\<local workspace>` and remove the G: project folders.
5. Completely exit and relaunch the app, then continue the existing chat.
6. Project-list tool reports the project's path as C:, but the sandbox setup log still tries to grant a write ACE on the previous G: workspace and fails.

## Errors
Shell:
```text
Failed to create unified exec process: helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors
```
Browser automation runtime:
```text
node_repl kernel exited unexpectedly
windows sandbox failed: helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors
```
Sanitized sandbox log excerpt:
```text
[2026-10-07T07:58:20.021997400+00:00] granting write ACE to G:\<Google Drive folder>\<Unicode workspace> for sandbox group and capability SID
[2026-10-07T07:58:20.032892400+00:00] write ACE grant failed on G:\<Google Drive folder>\<Unicode workspace>: SetSecurityInfo failed: 87
setup refresh: processed 3 write roots (read roots delegated); errors=["write ACE failed on G:\\<Google Drive folder>\\<Unicode workspace>: SetSecurityInfo failed: 87"]
setup refresh completed with errors
setup error: setup refresh had errors
```

## Additional diagnostics
- Explicitly setting shell working directory to C: did not reliably resolve the error. A simple Get-Location check succeeded once for both C: and G:, but subsequent file listing and browser runtime startup failed again. This intermittency is not understood.
- An approved `require_escalated` shell execution successfully listed the G: source folder and wrote a Markdown handoff note to C:. This confirms the original user context can access the files; it does not establish sandbox access.
- No sandbox configuration, Windows ACLs, helper executables or protected folders were modified as a workaround.
- A fresh C:-based chat was created as a possible recovery path, but its recovery status was not verified when this report was submitted.

## Expected behavior
A virtual-drive permission setup failure should produce an actionable error identifying the unsupported root instead of disabling unrelated file/browser tools with `helper_unknown_error`. After changing project folders, existing chats should either refresh their sandbox roots or clearly explain that the original chat workspace is retained and provide a supported migration/recovery action.

## Impact / investigation request
Ordinary monthly document preparation and browser workflow inspection are blocked despite the documents and browser page remaining accessible in the desktop UI. Please investigate Google Drive write-root ACL compatibility and whether retaining the former G: workspace in an existing chat after project changes is intended behavior or a stale-root bug.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Not captured for this incident. A version from an earlier incident has intentionally not been reused.

### What subscription do you have?

Not captured in this report.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS desktop, with a local Codex task coordinated through dot. Exact macOS version, architecture, app build, and affected model were not captured for this incident.

### What issue are you seeing?

During a local task on October 7, 2026, a browser `pageAssets.bundle` operation stalled for approximately 52 minutes. Follow-up messages submitted to the active task were acknowledged with `admissionOutcome: "steered"`, but there was no reliable indication that the task had actually received or processed them. When execution resumed, many of those follow-ups reached the task together.

The coordination problem is the combination of a long-running/blocked tool, ambiguous steering acknowledgement, stale progress visibility, and a backlog of increasingly outdated instructions on recovery.

Importantly, dot sent the repeated status checks and recovery instructions. The system did not independently generate those messages. Those repeated sends increased the backlog and made recovery noisier. This report does not establish duplicate delivery, message loss, or that any outdated instruction was actually executed.

#### Observed timeline

Approximate times below are UTC:

- Around 06:55: the local task stopped making visible progress during browser asset bundling.
- Around 07:00, 07:08, 07:16, 07:23, 07:30, and 07:34: dot sent follow-ups to the in-progress task. Submission responses reported `steered`.
- During the stall, persisted task-history reads lagged behind current activity; one read still surfaced a latest message from around 06:39. This made it difficult to distinguish a blocked task from a stale history projection.
- Around 07:36–07:37: read/wait task operations and diagnostic shell commands remained responsive. The task was still reported as active/inProgress with a null error. An inspected shell-command history contained 154 completed/failed commands and no command marked running. This does **not** rule out an outstanding browser/MCP operation.
- Around 07:48: the original task resumed and received many follow-ups submitted since approximately 07:00. It reported that the `pageAssets.bundle` call had been blocked for 3,122 seconds, and that no production writes had occurred during that blocked interval.

Sanitized summary of observed fields, not a raw trace:

```text
follow-up admissionOutcome: steered
task status during the stall: active / inProgress
task error: null
browser bundle elapsed time reported after recovery: 3122 seconds
```

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

No deterministic minimal reproduction is established. The observed sequence was:

1. Run a local Codex task on macOS that uses a browser tool.
2. A `pageAssets.bundle` call remains outstanding for an unusually long time.
3. Send several follow-ups to that active task through dot while the call is stalled.
4. Observe successful `steered` admission responses, without confirmation of task-side consumption or a clear blocked/waiting state.
5. Read task status/history while waiting; the task continues to appear in progress, and surfaced history can be stale.
6. When the tool call finally returns, observe the accumulated follow-ups becoming available together.

The trigger for the long tool stall is unknown. A permission wait was suspected, but not verified. No permission failure, browser deadlock, network cause, or shared root cause with other reports is established.

### What is the expected behavior?

- Show whether an active task is executing a tool, waiting for approval, waiting for a tool response, or unable to make progress, when that state is known.
- Distinguish message acceptance/queueing from delivery and consumption. A `steered` acknowledgement should have clear semantics and should not be the only available evidence when consumption is delayed.
- Expose pending follow-ups and their delivery state, with supported ways to cancel or replace superseded instructions.
- Make stale history/progress reads identifiable rather than presenting an old snapshot as current.
- On recovery, preserve message order and allow obsolete status checks or superseded instructions to be reconciled before they cause unintended work. This should not silently discard distinct user instructions.
- Surface an actionable timeout or recovery option for a prolonged tool wait.

### Additional information

Related reports checked before filing:

- #51251: Steer/queued submissions fail before dispatch with “Queued follow-up changed before dispatch.” Here, submissions returned `steered`, followed by delayed task-side receipt during a long tool call.
- #49456: accepted inputs remain visibly queued and receipt/snapshot reconciliation is inconsistent. This may be relevant to the stale-history aspect, but a shared cause is unproven.
- #51039: a completed tool operation was delayed at outer dispatch until a WebSocket timeout. This incident does not have the host-versus-dispatch timing evidence needed to establish the same mechanism.

Private task contents, websites, local addresses, filesystem paths, account data, session identifiers, credentials, and raw conversation screenshots are omitted. The original task recovered, but the cause and reproducibility remain unknown.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.930.61225 (13232)

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro 200

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 arm

### What issue are you seeing?

My disk lost about 20 GB in one night to `~/.codex/.tmp/marketplaces/.staging`.

The cause is one git marketplace whose upstream repo renamed its marketplace. microsoft/Webwright changed the `name` in `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` from `webwright` to `cuawright` on 2026-10-05 (commit 69922bc). My `config.toml` still had `[marketplaces.webwright]`. Since then every auto-upgrade clones the repo into a new `marketplace-upgrade-*` folder, reads the new name, and fails:

```
WARN codex_core_plugins::manager: failed to auto-upgrade configured marketplace marketplace="webwright" error=upgraded marketplace name `cuawright` does not match configured marketplace `webwright`
```

The 151 MB clone is never removed, and the upgrade runs again at the next session start or refresh. With a few Codex sessions open that came to about 130 clones overnight. The name will never match again, so the loop doesn't stop until someone notices the disk.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Configure a git marketplace whose repo later renames its marketplace, e.g. `[marketplaces.webwright]` with `source = "https://github.com/microsoft/Webwright.git"` (now named `cuawright`).
2. Keep Codex running and open a few sessions over a few hours.
3. `ls ~/.codex/.tmp/marketplaces/.staging | wc -l` grows by one full clone per upgrade attempt, and the log shows the name-mismatch warning each time.

### What is the expected behavior?

- A failed upgrade removes its staging clone.
- A name mismatch is treated as permanent: Codex stops retrying it and tells me the marketplace was renamed upstream (ideally offering to switch to the new name), instead of trying again on every start.

### Additional information

The staging leak in general is already tracked in #21005 and #39421. This is a way to hit it that never stops by itself, since the error can't clear.

Separately, this marketplace's plugin uses a `github` source, which Codex skips (`skipping marketplace plugin with unsupported source`), so the entry never installed anything in Codex either.

items.body:
Distinguish thread listing failures from exhausted history

## Why

DB-only listing and pagination failures must not look like exhausted history. This hardens the DB-only listing added in https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/18502 and page refilling added in https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/7509.

## What changed

- Return JSON-RPC error `-32603` when `useStateDbOnly: true` cannot query the local state database, including requests with an empty `cwd` array.
- Track all cursors encountered while filling a page and return `-32603` for repeated cursors, including on full pages.
- Document that callers can retry these errors; a successful response with `nextCursor: null` still indicates exhaustion. Default scan-and-repair requests retain their filesystem fallback.

## Testing

Add regression tests for missing or mismatched state databases versus healthy empty history, with active and archived listings and null or empty `cwd` filters. Cover repeated cursors during page refilling and on full pages using the in-memory thread store.

items.body:
Title: Windows app 26.1002.51308: sandbox setup fails with sharing violation when validating its own active runtime

## Summary

After updating the Windows Codex app to 26.1002.51308 (build 13417), all command execution fails before the requested command starts:

```text
helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors
```

Node REPL also fails:

```text
trusted Node process exited unexpectedly
```

Sandbox logs show that runtime ACL validation attempts to open files currently used by Codex itself and fails with Windows error 32 (`ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION`).

## Environment

- OS: Windows
- Codex app: 26.1002.51308, build 13417
- Windows sandbox: elevated
- Previous helper directory: `Codex\bin\5ea220ae823df3d7`
- Previous command-runner version: 0.160.1
- Current helper directory: `Codex\bin\979a96ce184041d1`
- Current runtime: `cua_node\2c9e75c4e9c71beb`

## Expected behavior

Sandbox setup should complete while Codex's own runtime processes are running. Commands and Node REPL should start normally.

## Actual behavior

Every command fails during sandbox setup refresh. The relevant log entry is:

```text
runtime read/execute validation failed: validate runtime read/execute access on
C:\Users\<USER>\AppData\Local\OpenAI\Codex\runtimes\cua_node\2c9e75c4e9c71beb\bin\node_repl.exe:
open ACL target for root-only update: The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process. (os error 32)
```

After stopping the two `node_repl.exe` processes during an earlier diagnostic test, validation passed that file but failed with the same error on:

```text
...\bin\node_modules\@oai\sky\bin\windows\swift\x64\VCRUNTIME140_1.dll
```

Stopping those processes did not resolve the issue.

## Regression evidence

From `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\.sandbox\sandbox.2026-10-07.log`:

- Previous helper: 50 successful setup refreshes, no failures.
- Current helper: 13 failed setup refreshes, no successes.
- Latest recorded failure: October 7, 2026, 15:05 JST.
- Logs from October 6 and earlier contain no `runtime read/execute validation` entries.

Both restarting the app and rebooting Windows failed to resolve the problem. No newer app update was available when checked.

## Diagnostic findings

- There is only one runtime under `runtimes`: `cua_node\2c9e75c4e9c71beb`.
- There are no old runtime directories or `.staging-*` directories.
- Therefore, the stale-runtime workaround described in #44696 does not apply here.
- Processes using the affected runtime include Codex's own `node_repl.exe`, `node.exe`, and `codex-computer-use-swift.exe`.
- Read and execute permissions for the sandbox group are already present.
- The earlier, separate error 5 / `helper_sandbox_lock_failed` issue has been resolved.
- A separate error 32 involving `C:\Users\<USER>` is followed by `continuing setup`; it is not the fatal failure described above.

The latest investigation was read-only. No files, configuration, or permissions were changed.

## Suspected cause — not confirmed

Based on the public `openai/codex` main branch inspected on October 7, 2026:

In `codex-rs/windows-sandbox-rs/src/acl.rs`, `ensure_allow_mask_aces_with_inheritance_impl` opens a target with `OpenOptions` and `access_mode(MAXIMUM_ALLOWED)` when `inheritance == 0`, using the context:

```text
open ACL target for root-only update
```

In `setup_provisioning/setup_runtime_bin.rs`, `ensure_runtime_tree_readable` calls `grant_read_execute_aces(..., 0)` for files throughout the runtime tree.

My hypothesis is that requesting `MAXIMUM_ALLOWED` may include write access when opening running executables or loaded DLLs, causing a sharing violation. That validation error then causes the entire setup refresh to fail, blocking all command execution.

This is an inference from the logs and public source, not a confirmed root cause. I have not verified that the public main branch exactly matches the installed app build.

## Possible fix directions

Please consider whether ACL inspection can open targets with `READ_CONTROL` only, requesting `WRITE_DAC` separately only when an ACL change is actually needed.

It may also be worth reviewing how validation handles files already in use by Codex. Any handling of sharing violations should preserve the required sandbox access checks rather than simply bypassing them.

## Related issue

#44696 reports runtime validation failures, but its stale-runtime workaround does not match this environment.

## Actual behavior and reproduction

On the affected existing installation, ask the desktop chat or its programming subagent to run a normal PowerShell `Get-Location`. Execution fails before the command starts:

```text
exec-server rejected request (-32603):
helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors
```

```text
runtime read/execute validation failed
open ACL target for root-only update
The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process. (os error 32)
setup refresh: exited with status ExitStatus(ExitStatus(1))
```

The target was first `VCRUNTIME140_1.dll` under the bundled cua_node/sky Swift runtime, then `node_repl.exe` under the same runtime. A separate profile-directory error was marked `continuing setup`; executable validation was in the fatal errors list.

Repeated app updates and reported restarts/reboots did not restore this chat. A single targeted stop of `codex-computer-use-swift` did not restore it; a later instance was observed. No kill loop was performed. An earlier, distinct `helper_sandbox_lock_failed` on `.sandbox-bin` temporarily responded to a backed-up, directory-only SYSTEM-WDAC addition; setup removed that right again. This was not a lasting fix for the current sharing violation. No recursive ACL reset, owner change, runtime replacement or sandbox disabling was performed.

## Separate stable comparison

The user ran the official portable 0.160.1 package:

```text
codex.exe sandbox --permission-profile ':read-only' --include-managed-config --cd <test-directory> -- powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command Get-Location
```

Output: `C:\`; exit code: `0`. Immediately afterwards, one normal probe each in the original chat and subagent still failed before execution. These are different execution contexts, not a controlled identical A/B test. No Git/compiler/engine readiness or permanent desktop repair is inferred. A separate programming chat has since resumed work according to the user; its runtime was not independently verified here.

## Source hypothesis, not proven root cause

The exact [0.162.0-alpha.2 acl.rs](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.0-alpha.2/codex-rs/windows-sandbox-rs/src/acl.rs) contains a root-only open using `MAXIMUM_ALLOWED` before the DACL/no-op check and the matching error context. That additional branch is absent from the checked [0.160.1 acl.rs](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.1/codex-rs/windows-sandbox-rs/src/acl.rs). Please investigate access requirements for live runtime files. The installed setup-helper binary has not been hash/debugger-matched to that source.

## Impact and requested outcome

Basic commands are blocked, while repeated manual log collection and unsuccessful recovery consume substantial user time and chat context. Exact token/cost totals have not been measured. The user considers this burden unacceptable for routine tasks.

Please provide a supported desktop fix or stable-runtime route, surface the actual file/Win32 failure directly, and offer a single sanitized diagnostic export instead of repeated manual diagnosis and generic restart advice.

Related report: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/51590. This report adds the separate stable comparison; the other reporter's measurements are not attributed to this installation. No clean-install reproduction established.

items.title: Add thread ID exclusions to `thread/list`
items.body:
Add thread ID exclusions to `thread/list`

## Why

Clients displaying a saved manual thread order need to list the remaining threads without repeating those already loaded separately.

## What changed

Add optional `excludedThreadIds` to `thread/list` and the generated protocol bindings. Apply exclusions before the result limit, refilling pages until the requested limit is reached or history is exhausted while preserving existing filters and ordering. Clients must send the same exclusions on each page.

Accept up to 100 entries, counting duplicates toward the bound. Reject invalid IDs or oversized lists with JSON-RPC error `-32602` rather than truncating them. Omitted, null, and empty lists preserve existing behavior.

## Testing

Add integration coverage for page refill across database-only and scan/repair paths, archived threads, sort directions, and project/section scopes. Cover duplicate and unknown IDs, the 100-entry boundary, invalid input, and preservation of section order.

### What issue are you seeing?

After updating and restarting the Windows desktop app on October 7, 2026, I can no longer submit the **first message of a new Work conversation** from the ChatGPT → Work home screen.

- **Existing Work conversations can still receive follow-up messages.**
- **Codex mode can still send messages normally.**

This is therefore different from the older “first turn succeeds, second turn cannot be sent” reports: the new Work entry point is blocked before its first turn, while existing Work conversations remain usable.

1. Open the Windows desktop app and select ChatGPT → Work.
2. Start a new Work conversation from the home screen.
3. Select “Run on your computer”.
4. Select a model and enter a short text prompt.
5. Observe that Send remains disabled and Enter does not submit.
6. Switch to cloud execution or select another model: the first prompt remains blocked.
7. Open an existing Work conversation and send a follow-up: it works.
8. Switch to Codex and send a prompt: it works.

Local log inspection indicated a task-resumption path mixing a POSIX-style `/tmp/.../workspace/` prefix with a Windows `C:\Users\<redacted>\...` path. The Windows part exists on the affected PC. labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request
